clinicalPearls: A rare but potentially fatal disorder marked by acute non-inflammatory encephalopathy occurring alongside fatty change in the liver and other organs.
Classically follows a viral illness, especially influenza or varicella, during the recovery phase.
Salicylate (aspirin) exposure during a preceding viral infection is a well-recognised association, and the sharp decline in incidence tracks with public advice to avoid aspirin in children.
Typical evolution is protracted vomiting followed by progressive neurological deterioration: irritability or lethargy advancing to confusion, delirium, seizures, and coma.
Liver dysfunction is present but jaundice is characteristically absent or minimal, which can be a useful discriminating clue.
Laboratory findings include raised transaminases, hyperammonaemia, prolonged prothrombin time, and often hypoglycaemia in younger children.
In any child presenting with this picture, an underlying inborn error of metabolism (particularly a fatty acid oxidation or urea cycle defect) must be excluded, as these mimic Reye syndrome.
Management is supportive with a focus on controlling raised intracranial pressure, correcting metabolic derangements, and protecting cerebral perfusion.
Prognosis correlates strongly with the depth of coma and the degree of hyperammonaemia at presentation.
reference.pathophysiology: The core lesion is acute, generalised mitochondrial injury. Diffuse mitochondrial dysfunction in the liver impairs the urea cycle and fatty acid oxidation, producing microvesicular fatty infiltration of hepatocytes, hyperammonaemia, and disturbed intermediary metabolism. In the brain this mitochondrial failure, combined with hyperammonaemia, drives cytotoxic cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressure, which underlie the encephalopathy. Salicylate metabolites are thought to potentiate mitochondrial injury in susceptible children following a viral trigger.
additionalDifferentials: Inborn errors of metabolism (fatty acid oxidation defects, urea cycle disorders, organic acidaemias)
additionalInvestigations: Liver transaminases, bilirubin, and coagulation profile
Metabolic screen: plasma amino acids, urine organic acids, acylcarnitine profile
Neuroimaging to assess cerebral oedema and exclude other causes
Lumbar puncture only when safe and to exclude CNS infection
Liver biopsy in atypical or diagnostically uncertain cases
redFlags: Rapidly progressive encephalopathy or declining conscious level (EMERGENCY)
Signs of raised intracranial pressure: abnormal posturing, pupillary changes, bradycardia with hypertension
Progression to coma requiring airway protection and intensive care
reference.prognosis: Outcome depends heavily on how advanced the encephalopathy is at presentation; children who remain in earlier stages often recover well, whereas deep coma and severe hyperammonaemia carry high risk of death or lasting neurological deficit. Early recognition and aggressive management of intracranial pressure improve survival.
pitfalls: Attributing the illness to Reye syndrome without excluding an inborn error of metabolism, which is now a more common cause of this presentation
Being reassured by absent jaundice despite significant hepatic derangement
Delaying management of raised intracranial pressure while awaiting confirmatory tests
Overlooking hypoglycaemia, especially in infants and young children
Failing to elicit a history of aspirin or salicylate-containing product use
management: Avoid salicylates in children with viral illness, the key preventive measure
Manage in intensive care with aggressive control of raised intracranial pressure and cerebral oedema
Correct hypoglycaemia and metabolic derangement with intravenous dextrose-containing fluids
Correct coagulopathy with vitamin K and blood products as needed
Lower ammonia and support the failing liver with supportive measures
Exclude inherited metabolic mimics such as fatty acid oxidation and urea cycle defects with a metabolic screen
Monitor neurological status closely and escalate neuroprotective measures as the encephalopathy advances
